title: A Family Office Is a Set of Functions, Not a Building
summary: A family office is whatever arrangement performs five functions for a family's wealth: setting policy, investing, accounting and reporting, managing advisers, and administering the family's affairs. This lesson separates those functions, introduces the investment policy statement, and shows a small family how to start.
body:
You do not need a building, a staff or a fortune to have a family office. You need five functions performed deliberately, and one document, the investment policy statement, that tells everyone how the money is to be managed.

Recall

Q. What makes a family constitution's rules enforceable?

A. Carrying each principle into an implementing document, such as the shareholders' agreement, articles, trust deed or will. The constitution itself is usually non-binding by design.

Q. Why might an estate need probate in more than one country?

A. Because each jurisdiction where assets sit may require its own grant, or local recognition of a foreign one, before the executor can deal with those assets.

Q. What is personal leverage, and why does it raise risk?

A. Borrowing that you are personally liable for, including guarantees. It magnifies gains and losses, and a loss can reach assets outside the project.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a developer who succeeds ends up with wealth in many places: project companies, rental buildings, cash from a sale, investments, insurance, and perhaps assets in two countries. Each piece has its own adviser, its own statement and its own deadline. Without someone coordinating, nobody sees the whole picture, fees accumulate unnoticed, and decisions are made by whichever adviser calls first. That coordination is what a family office does. Nadia joins me this week because most of it rests on accounting and reporting.

The five functions

Plain English. A family office is the arrangement that manages a family's wealth and affairs as a whole, rather than asset by asset. A large one may employ dozens of people. A small one may be one part-time bookkeeper, a spreadsheet and an annual meeting. What makes it a family office is the functions it performs, not its size.

The five functions are these. Policy: deciding the goals, risk limits and rules for the wealth. Investment: choosing and monitoring where money goes, whether done in-house or delegated. Accounting and reporting: recording every asset and liability and producing one consolidated view. Adviser management: hiring, instructing, reviewing and replacing lawyers, accountants, managers and insurers. Administration: tax filings, insurance renewals, entity maintenance, bill payment and the family's paperwork.

The professional framing distinguishes a single-family office, which serves one family; a multi-family office, a firm that serves several families and shares its costs among them; and what is often called a virtual family office, in which the family coordinates outside providers without employing staff. For most developers at an early stage the virtual model is the realistic one.

Applied example, hypothetical. A family holds two rental buildings, a holding company with cash from a sale, a personal investment account, and life insurance. A virtual family office here is: an outside accountant who prepares one consolidated quarterly report; the investment manager, instructed by a written policy; the estate lawyer, on an annual review; and the developer himself, who chairs a quarterly meeting and owns the policy. Total staff employed: none.

The investment policy statement

An investment policy statement, usually shortened to IPS, is a written document that sets the purpose of a pool of money, its return objective, its risk tolerance, its constraints, how it is to be allocated, and how and by whom its performance will be reviewed. Institutions such as pension funds and endowments have used them for a long time; families borrow the practice.

Its value is that it decides calmly, in advance, what you will do in a panic. When markets fall, the question is not "what do I feel like doing?" but "what does the policy say?" It also turns an adviser's job into something you can measure: did they follow the policy?

A typical IPS answers seven questions. What is this money for? What return do we need, after fees, tax and inflation? How much loss can we tolerate, in money and in time? What must we keep liquid, and when? What constraints apply: tax, legal, ethical, family? How is the money divided among asset types, with ranges? Who reviews it, how often, and against what benchmark?

Say that out loud now.

Applied example, hypothetical. A family sells a building and has 4,000,000 dollars of cash. Its IPS says: purpose, fund the founder's retirement and a reserve for future projects; liquidity, 500,000 dollars always in cash for project equity calls; tolerance, no more than a 15 percent decline in any one year without a review; constraint, no single holding above 10 percent; review, quarterly against a stated benchmark. Now every proposal from an adviser is tested against those lines. This is a conceptual illustration; no product, fund or security is being recommended, and a licensed adviser is required before you act.

Who owns the office

One more first principle: the office serves the family, so the family must own its decisions. A common failure in small family offices is that the most capable adviser gradually becomes the office: the accountant who also suggests investments, or the manager who also prepares the summary the family reads. Nobody planned it; it was convenient. The test is simple. Ask, for each of the five functions, whose name is on it, and whether that person is paid in a way that depends on the answer they give you. An adviser paid more when you invest more should not also be the one telling you how much to invest.

Applied example, hypothetical. A developer's long-time accountant offers to place his surplus cash with a manager the accountant introduces, and to report on it as part of the quarterly accounts. It is efficient and friendly. It also puts referral, oversight and reporting in one pair of hands. The better arrangement keeps the accountant on reporting, reconciled to the custodian, and selects any manager through a separate process the developer runs.

How the best do it

The practice that distinguishes well-run institutional investors, which I describe without naming any, is separation of duties. The people who decide policy are not the people who pick investments, and neither is the person who holds the assets or counts the results. Custody is with an independent institution, reporting is prepared from the custodian's records rather than the manager's, and the policy is reviewed annually by people who have no fee riding on the answer. A small family can copy this cheaply: keep assets with an independent custodian, have your accountant reconcile to the custodian's statements, and never let one adviser be policy-setter, manager and reporter at once. Day 2 shows what happens when that separation is missing.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: the office's job is to see the after-tax result across all entities and accounts, not each in isolation; verify any rule against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: keep operating risk in project companies and passive wealth outside them. Banking: one consolidated statement of net worth makes every loan application faster and more credible. Governance: the IPS and a written list of who may approve what are the office's constitution. Estate: the office keeps the asset register your executor will need. Exit: when a project sells, the IPS already says where the proceeds go.

Professional sign-off required: accountant, on consolidated reporting; licensed investment adviser, on any allocation; estate lawyer, on how assets are held.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is fragmentation: each adviser managing their own piece, nobody seeing the whole, and the family's real risk and real fees invisible. The control is one consolidated report, a written IPS, and a named person, usually you, accountable for coordinating the advisers.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking a family office begins when the wealth is large enough to hire staff. The functions are needed as soon as you hold assets in more than one place. Start with the policy and the consolidated report; hire later if the work demands it.

Callback

In Week 85, Warrick introduced ownership layers, liquidity tiers and currency reserves as the architecture of wealth. The family office is the building's operations team. The architecture says where things sit; the office makes sure someone looks at all of it, every quarter, against a written policy.

Recap

A family office is five functions: policy, investment, accounting and reporting, adviser management and administration. The investment policy statement decides in calm what you will do in a panic. Separate the duties of deciding, managing, holding and counting.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: the Madoff fraud and what independent custody would have caught.
checklist: I can name who performs each of the five family office functions for me.
I have a written investment policy statement for each pool of money.
My IPS states purpose, return need, loss tolerance, liquidity, constraints, allocation and review.
My assets are held by an independent custodian.
My reports are reconciled to custodian statements, not manager statements.
No single adviser sets policy, manages money and reports results.
I chair a review of the whole picture at least quarterly.
head: Field checklist
speak: A family office is not a building or a staff. It is five functions performed deliberately: policy, investment, accounting and reporting, managing advisers, and administration. A large family may employ people for each; a developer starting out can run a virtual family office by coordinating an accountant, an investment manager and a lawyer, with himself as chair. The core document is the investment policy statement. It states what the money is for, the return needed after fees, tax and inflation, how much loss can be tolerated, what must stay liquid, the constraints, the allocation ranges, and who reviews performance against what. It decides in calm what you will do in a panic, and it makes each adviser's job measurable. The best institutions separate duties: policy, management, custody and reporting sit with different people. Copy that, and keep your assets with an independent custodian.
terms: Family office — the arrangement, of any size, that manages a family's wealth and affairs as a whole rather than asset by asset.
Investment policy statement (IPS) — a written document setting a pool of money's purpose, return objective, risk tolerance, constraints, allocation and review process.
Separation of duties — assigning policy, investment management, custody and reporting to different people so no one can both act and report on their own actions.

hostile.q: You say you have a family office. Who actually holds your liquid assets, and who checks the statements?
hostile.a: An independent custodian holds them, in accounts in our entities' names. My accountant reconciles the quarterly report to the custodian's own statements, not to the manager's, and I review the reconciliation. No adviser both manages and reports on the same money.

title: Madoff: When the Manager Also Held and Counted the Money
summary: The Bernard Madoff fraud, exposed in December 2008, survived for years because one firm managed the money, held it and reported on it, with an auditor too small to check. Seven forensic steps show the warning signs and the separation of duties that would have caught it.
body:
Madoff's investors were not fooled by a complex product. They were fooled by an arrangement in which the same firm chose the investments, held the assets and produced the statements, so the only evidence that the money existed came from the person taking it.

Recall

Q. In the equalisation example, what is sweat equity?

A. Value attributed to an heir's underpaid or unpaid work in the business, agreed in writing as a share of growth, and deducted before the rest of the estate is divided.

Q. What usually goes wrong when a person with assets in two countries relies on one will drafted for one of them?

A. The will may be slow or difficult to prove in the other country, may not suit its formalities or rules, and can leave assets frozen while a foreign grant is recognised.

Q. What is concentration risk on a personal balance sheet?

A. Having much of your wealth in one asset, market or currency, so a single event can damage most of it at once.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman joins me because this is a failure of wealth management, not of investing skill. When you build a family office, the single most important design choice is who holds the assets and who tells you what they are worth. This case shows what happens when the answer to both is "the manager". I will keep to facts I am confident of and describe the rest without figures.

1. Timeline

Bernard Madoff ran a securities firm in New York and, alongside it, an investment advisory business that for decades reported steady, positive returns to its clients. Many invested through feeder funds: other funds that placed their clients' money with Madoff. In 2000, and again in later submissions including a detailed memorandum in 2005, a financial analyst named Harry Markopolos told the United States Securities and Exchange Commission that the returns could not be genuine. The regulator examined the firm more than once without uncovering the fraud. In late 2008, during the financial crisis, clients asked for withdrawals the firm could not meet. On 11 December 2008 Madoff was arrested, after admitting to family members that the advisory business was a fraud. He pleaded guilty in March 2009 and was sentenced in June 2009 to 150 years in prison. Reported account balances ran to tens of billions of dollars, most of it fictitious.

2. Key decisions

Investors made three decisions that mattered. They accepted that Madoff's own firm would hold their assets, rather than an independent custodian. They accepted statements and trade confirmations produced by the same firm. And many invested through feeder funds that took fees for access and, in some cases, performed little independent checking of their own.

3. Assumptions

Investors assumed that a long record of returns was evidence of skill. They assumed that a prominent figure in the securities industry, once a chairman of an industry exchange, would not run a fraud. They assumed that a regulated firm was a checked firm. And they assumed that someone else, the feeder fund, the auditor or the regulator, had done the diligence they had not.

4. Incentives

Feeder funds earned fees on money they placed, so their incentive was to keep placing it. Investors enjoying smooth returns had little incentive to ask hard questions. Madoff's firm had every incentive to keep inflows exceeding withdrawals, because, as in any Ponzi scheme, new money paid old investors. Nobody in the chain was paid to be sceptical except the analyst who was not paid at all.

Say that out loud now.

5. Warning signs ignored

First, returns that were too smooth: steady monthly gains with almost no losing months, for a strategy that should have fluctuated with markets. Second, self-custody: assets held by the manager's own firm. Third, an auditor that was a very small firm, far too small to audit an operation of that size. Fourth, a refusal to explain the strategy in detail, presented as secrecy that protected an edge. Fifth, the repeated written warnings to the regulator. Any one of these deserved a question; together they described the structure of a fraud.

6. Point of no return

For each investor, the point of no return was the moment money went into an account whose existence could only be confirmed by the manager. After that, the investor had no independent way to know the truth. For the scheme as a whole, the end came when withdrawals in a crisis exceeded new money, which in a Ponzi scheme is not a risk but a certainty, only a question of when.

7. Root cause

The root cause was the absence of separation of duties. One firm decided, executed, held and reported. Every other failure, the smooth returns, the tiny auditor, the feeder funds' thin diligence, would have been caught by one fact: an independent custodian sending statements directly to the investor, which the investor or their accountant reconciled to the manager's reports. Fraud needs the manager to control the evidence. Independent custody removes that control.

The check an ordinary investor could have made

It is worth asking what a careful individual, with no special access, could have done. Markopolos's core argument, as widely reported, was that the strategy described could not produce the returns reported, and that the trading it implied should have been visible in the markets and was not. Most investors could not have run that analysis. But every investor could have asked three plain questions. Who holds my assets, and can I contact them directly? Who audits the firm, and how large is that auditor? Can you show me a losing month and explain it? An honest manager can answer all three in a day. An answer that is evasive, or that relies on the manager's reputation in place of a document, is itself the finding. You do not need to understand a strategy to notice that nobody independent is checking it.

What a family office copies

Roman's translation into practice. First, every asset sits with an independent custodian, in an account in the family's own name or entity's name. Second, the custodian sends statements to you or your accountant directly, not via the manager. Third, someone without a fee interest reconciles the two each quarter. Fourth, any return pattern that is smoother than its strategy should allow is investigated, not celebrated. Fifth, if you invest through an intermediary, you ask it to show you its own diligence on the underlying manager, in writing. This is conceptual; no product or manager is recommended, and a licensed adviser is required before you act.

Professional sign-off required: licensed investment adviser, on the custody and reporting arrangement; accountant, on the quarterly reconciliation.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk in any family office is trusting a person's reputation in place of an independent record. The control is structural: independent custody, direct statements and an independent reconciliation, which work even when your judgement of people fails.

The beginner's mistake

Treating consistently good returns as reassurance. Unusually steady returns are a reason for more scrutiny, not less, and the question to ask is "how could this strategy produce this pattern?"

Callback

In Week 61, Cole taught arm's-length dealing and documentation in intercompany transactions: a transaction is credible when an independent party could check it. Madoff's statements failed exactly that test. No one independent of the manager could verify a single trade, and the family office's whole job is to make sure every number it relies on can be checked by someone who is not paid to produce it.

Recap

Madoff's advisory business reported steady returns for years, held its own clients' assets, issued its own statements and used a tiny auditor. Warnings reached the regulator from 2000 onward; the fraud collapsed in December 2008 when withdrawals outran new money. The root cause was one firm deciding, holding and reporting.

Rule 94: Never let the person who manages your money also hold it or report on it; keep every asset with an independent custodian whose statements reach you directly and are reconciled each quarter.

Next: Nadia, on The Money: what a family office costs, in fees and in basis points, and when it pays for itself.
checklist: Every investment asset sits with an independent custodian in my or my entity's name.
Custodian statements reach me or my accountant directly.
Someone with no fee interest reconciles custodian and manager reports quarterly.
I investigate any return pattern smoother than its strategy allows.
I ask any intermediary for its written diligence on the underlying manager.
I check that an auditor is of a size and standing to match the business it audits.
I never accept a refusal to explain a strategy as proof of an edge.
head: Field checklist
speak: Bernard Madoff ran an advisory business that reported steady returns for decades. His own firm held clients' assets and produced their statements, and the auditor was a very small firm. A financial analyst, Harry Markopolos, warned the regulator in 2000 and again in later submissions, including a detailed memorandum in 2005, without result. In the 2008 crisis, withdrawals exceeded new money; Madoff was arrested on 11 December 2008, pleaded guilty in March 2009 and was sentenced to 150 years that June. The warning signs were too-smooth returns, self-custody, a tiny auditor, a secret strategy and written warnings. The point of no return for each investor was money placed where only the manager could confirm it existed. The root cause was no separation of duties. Rule 94: never let the person who manages your money also hold it or report on it; use an independent custodian whose statements reach you directly and are reconciled each quarter.
terms: Custodian — an independent institution that holds investment assets in safekeeping in the owner's name and reports their holdings.
Ponzi scheme — a fraud in which returns to earlier investors are paid from new investors' money rather than from genuine profits.
Feeder fund — a fund that pools investors' money and places it with another manager, earning fees for access.

hostile.q: Your manager has beaten the market every year for ten years with almost no down months. Why are you not putting more in?
hostile.a: Because a pattern that smooth needs an explanation before it gets more money. I will first confirm the assets with the independent custodian directly, reconcile their statements to the manager's, and ask the manager to explain how the strategy produces that pattern. Until those three are done, the allocation stays at its policy limit.

rule: Rule 94: Never let the person who manages your money also hold it or report on it; keep every asset with an independent custodian whose statements reach you directly and are reconciled each quarter.

title: What a Family Office Costs, and the Fee You Never See
summary: A family office costs money in two ways: the visible cost of people and services, and the less visible drag of layered fees on returns, compounded over decades. This lesson prices both in basis points, shows when consolidating services pays, and adds the Wealth Ledger line for total cost of ownership.
body:
The cost of managing wealth is quoted in small percentages and paid in large sums. Add every layer of fee, express the total in basis points, and compound it over twenty years before you decide anything is cheap.

Recall

Q. In the family meeting, why stay silent after a sibling says "we're both your children"?

A. Because they have said the hardest thing in the room, and filling the silence with an explanation signals you were waiting to rebut them. Acknowledge it before answering.

Q. Why can probate in several countries be costly even when no tax is due?

A. Each grant may need local lawyers, translations, certified copies and court fees, and the delay itself can freeze assets that need managing or selling.

Q. In capital allocation, what does the size of a position decide?

A. How much a single loss can hurt you. Sizing caps the damage from being wrong, which matters more than how confident you are of being right.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, developers think hard about the cost of a construction loan and often not at all about the cost of managing the money a project eventually produces. Yet a fee of 1 percent a year, quoted casually, can consume a large share of the growth on a portfolio over a working life. This lesson makes those costs visible. All figures are hypothetical and illustrative.

Basis points and layers

A basis point is one hundredth of one percent: 100 basis points equal 1 percent. Professionals quote fees in basis points because the numbers are small and the differences between them matter.

The trap is layering: fees charged at more than one level on the same money. Suppose a family pays an adviser 75 basis points a year to manage its portfolio. The adviser invests through funds that each charge their own management fees, say 50 basis points on average. Some funds invest in other funds, adding another layer. There are trading costs, custody fees and the cost of preparing reports. The adviser quotes 75. The family actually pays the sum.

Applied example, hypothetical, on a 5,000,000 dollar portfolio.

LayerBasis pointsDollars a year
Adviser fee7537,500
Underlying fund fees5025,000
Custody and trading157,500
Accounting and reporting2010,000
Total16080,000

The quoted fee was 75 basis points. The total cost of ownership, every cost of owning and managing the assets expressed as one annual percentage, is 160 basis points, more than double.

Compounding the drag

Now compound it. Suppose the portfolio earns a gross return of 6 percent a year before costs. Over 20 years, ignoring tax and withdrawals:

At 6.0 percent net, 5,000,000 dollars grows to about 16,000,000 dollars. The multiplier is about 3.21.

At 4.4 percent net, after 160 basis points of cost, it grows to about 11,800,000 dollars. The multiplier is about 2.37.

The difference is roughly 4,200,000 dollars, on a starting sum of 5,000,000. Most of that difference is not the fees paid; it is the growth those fees would have earned. That is the fee you never see.

Say that out loud now.

The point is not that every fee is bad. Some services earn their cost several times over: a good tax adviser, a well-designed insurance structure, a custodian that prevents a fraud. The point is that every basis point should have a reason you can state, and the total should be known.

When consolidation pays

A family office often pays for itself by doing three things. It removes duplicate services, such as three accountants for three entities. It negotiates fees across the whole pool instead of piece by piece. And it prevents costly errors: missed tax elections, lapsed insurance, idle cash earning nothing.

Applied example, hypothetical. A family with 20,000,000 dollars spread across five advisers pays a total cost of ownership of 150 basis points, 300,000 dollars a year. It consolidates into one coordinated arrangement: a part-time controller at 90,000 dollars a year, one investment manager at a negotiated 60 basis points, and one accounting firm. New cost: roughly 90,000 plus 120,000 plus 40,000, about 250,000 dollars, or 125 basis points. Saving: about 50,000 dollars a year, before counting errors avoided. At 5,000,000 dollars of wealth, the same controller would cost 180 basis points on its own, and the arithmetic would not work. Scale decides whether people pay for themselves; at small scale, coordinate outside providers instead.

Percentage fees and flat fees

One more comparison, because the way a fee is charged changes its cost as you grow. A percentage-of-assets fee rises automatically as the portfolio rises, whether or not the work does. A flat annual fee stays the same. Hypothetical: an adviser charges 1 percent on 2,000,000 dollars, which is 20,000 dollars a year. Ten years later the portfolio is 6,000,000 dollars and the same 1 percent is 60,000 dollars, for broadly similar work. A flat fee of 25,000 dollars would have cost more at the start and far less by the end. Neither model is always better. Some families pay a percentage while the work is heavy and renegotiate to a flat fee once the portfolio matures. The discipline is to re-price the relationship every few years against the work actually being done.

Wealth Ledger

For your personal balance sheet, Mr Shabazz, add a line under net worth: total cost of ownership, in dollars and in basis points, across every entity and account. Ask each adviser to state every fee they receive, directly or indirectly, including fund-level fees and any referral payments, in writing once a year. Then compare the total to the value each provides. A balance sheet that shows assets and debts but not the annual cost of holding them is incomplete in the same way a pro forma without operating expenses would be.

Working with advisers

This month's thread. An adviser is a professional whose judgement you are buying and whose incentives you must understand. Before you take advice, ask how the adviser is paid, by whom, and whether the recommendation changes what they earn. Commission, a percentage of assets and a flat fee each pull in different directions, and none is wrong; what is wrong is not knowing which one you are dealing with.

Then manage advisers the way you manage a contractor: a written scope, a reporting rhythm, a review against the policy, and the willingness to replace one who drifts. Thank good advice and record it. Challenge advice you do not understand until you do, or until you decide it is not for you. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any investment, but the decision remains yours.

Professional sign-off required: accountant, on consolidated cost reporting; licensed investment adviser, on any change of manager or allocation.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is fee blindness: knowing the headline fee and not the total, so layered costs quietly consume much of a lifetime's growth. The control is an annual written fee disclosure from every adviser, consolidated into one total cost of ownership figure.

The beginner's mistake

Hiring staff too early to look like a family office. A salaried team costs a fixed sum, which at small scale is a large percentage. Start by coordinating outside providers; hire when the arithmetic shows the person saves more than they cost.

Callback

In Week 87, Warrick taught that fees and conflicts of interest matter as much as asset class when you invest beyond real estate. This lesson put a number on that idea. A 160 basis point total against a 75 basis point quote is not a detail; over twenty years it was worth most of the starting capital.

Recap

Fees are quoted in basis points and charged in layers. Add every layer into one total cost of ownership, compound it to see the growth it consumes, consolidate services when scale makes people pay for themselves, and know how every adviser is paid.

Next: Omar, on The Rules: fiduciary duty, conflicts and custody, the rules that govern the people managing your wealth.
checklist: I know my total cost of ownership in dollars and basis points.
Every adviser states all fees they receive, in writing, every year.
I include fund-level fees, custody, trading and reporting in the total.
I compound the total over twenty years before calling any fee cheap.
I can state a reason for every basis point I pay.
I consolidate services only when scale makes people pay for themselves.
I know how each adviser is paid and whether their advice changes their pay.
head: Field checklist
speak: Wealth management fees are quoted in basis points, a hundredth of a percent, and charged in layers. In a hypothetical 5,000,000 dollar portfolio, an adviser quotes 75 basis points, but underlying fund fees add 50, custody and trading 15, and reporting 20: a total cost of ownership of 160 basis points, 80,000 dollars a year. Compound it. At 6 percent gross, 5,000,000 grows to about 16,000,000 in twenty years; at 4.4 percent net of those costs, to about 11,800,000. The gap, roughly 4,200,000 dollars, is mostly growth the fees would have earned. Not every fee is bad; every fee needs a reason. A family office pays for itself by removing duplicate services, negotiating across the whole pool and preventing errors, but only at a scale where salaried people cost less than they save. Get every adviser's fees in writing once a year and know how each is paid.
terms: Basis point — one hundredth of one percent; 100 basis points equal 1 percent.
Fee layering — charging fees at more than one level on the same money, such as an adviser fee plus the fees of the funds the adviser selects.
Total cost of ownership — every cost of holding and managing an asset or portfolio, expressed as one annual figure or percentage.

hostile.q: Your adviser charges 75 basis points. That is competitive. Why are you asking for a full fee disclosure?
hostile.a: Because 75 is only the top layer. Once I add the underlying fund fees, custody, trading and reporting, my illustrative total is closer to 160, and over twenty years the difference is most of my starting capital. I need the full figure in writing to judge whether the value justifies it.

title: Duties, Conflicts and Custody: The Rules Around Your Advisers
summary: The people who manage a family's wealth are governed by duties of different strengths, by conflict rules, by licensing and by custody arrangements. This lesson explains those concepts, what an engagement letter should fix, and the governance a family office needs internally.
body:
Not every adviser owes you the same duty. Know which standard each one is held to, put the rest in the engagement letter, and give your own family office written rules on who may approve what.

Recall

Q. Name one defect in a family constitution clause that makes every child a director automatically.

A. It hands out board control with ownership regardless of ability or interest, which is the pattern behind deadlock. Board seats should follow a role, not a birth order.

Q. Why must multiple wills for different countries be drafted together?

A. So that one does not revoke the other through general revocation wording, and so every asset is covered once and only once.

Q. What is the danger of a personal guarantee in capital allocation terms?

A. It is leverage that reaches outside the project to your personal assets, so a project loss can become a personal one larger than the equity you chose to risk.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will hire people to manage, advise on and hold your wealth. The law places duties on them, but those duties differ by profession, by jurisdiction and by what the engagement says. Assuming every adviser must put your interests first is the most common and most expensive misunderstanding in this area. I teach concepts here; the standard that applies to any particular adviser depends on their licence and local law, so verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Strengths of duty

Plain English first. Some advisers must act in your best interest, putting your interests ahead of their own. Others must only recommend something suitable for you, which may still be the option that pays them more. Some, such as a salesperson for a product, may owe you little beyond honesty.

The professional framing uses the term fiduciary duty: a legal obligation to act loyally in another person's interest, to avoid or manage conflicts, and to exercise care. Trustees owe it. Directors owe it to their company. Many lawyers owe something close to it to their clients. Whether an investment adviser owes it depends on the type of licence, the jurisdiction and the service; regulatory regimes have used standards variously described as suitability, best interest and fiduciary, and the details change. A suitability standard, in general terms, requires that a recommendation fit the client's circumstances, without necessarily requiring that it be the best available for the client.

Applied example, hypothetical. Two advisers recommend similar funds. One is paid a flat fee and has accepted a written fiduciary obligation. The other is paid more if you buy one particular fund. Both recommendations may be legal. Only the first adviser has bound themselves to put your interest first. Ask each, in writing, which standard they accept for this engagement.

Conflicts of interest

A conflict of interest exists when an adviser's own interest could pull against yours: commissions, referral payments, in-house products, or a relationship with the other side of a transaction. Rules generally require conflicts to be disclosed, and some require them to be avoided or managed. Disclosure alone does not remove a conflict; it only tells you it is there.

Applied example. Your accountant introduces an insurance broker and receives a referral payment if you buy a policy. That is not necessarily improper. It is a fact you are entitled to know before you rely on the accountant's view that you need the policy. A family office rule might state: every adviser discloses, in writing, any payment they receive that depends on our decisions, and any adviser with such a payment does not give the deciding opinion on that decision.

Say that out loud now.

Licensing, custody and the engagement letter

Many activities, such as giving investment advice, managing money for others, selling insurance or dealing in securities, are generally licensed or registered activities. Before you engage someone, confirm they hold the licence for the service they are providing, in the jurisdiction they are providing it. A licence does not guarantee competence; its absence is a reason to stop.

Custody rules, in many places, govern how a manager that holds or controls client assets must protect them, for example through qualified custodians and independent verification. Day 2's case is the reason they exist. Your own structure should not depend on those rules alone: insist on an independent custodian whatever the minimum requirement.

The engagement letter, from Week 25, is where the rest is fixed. For a wealth adviser it should state the scope of services, the standard of duty accepted, every form of compensation, how conflicts are handled, who holds the assets, what reports you receive and how often, confidentiality, how either side ends the relationship, and what happens to your records when it ends.

Applied example, hypothetical. A developer sells a building and engages a wealth manager by signing a two-page account form. A year later he discovers the manager also earns a share of the fees of the funds it chose for him, and that the form allowed it. Nothing illegal happened. What was missing was an engagement letter he had negotiated: one that named the duty, listed every source of pay, and required written notice before any in-house product was used. The fix costs an hour of a lawyer's time before signing, against years of undisclosed cost after.

Governance inside the family office

The family office needs its own rules, separate from what advisers owe you. Three are essential. First, an approval matrix: a written table of who may approve which decisions up to what amount, and which need two signatures. Second, a conflicts register for family members as well as advisers, because a family member may have an interest too. Third, a records rule: where every agreement, statement and policy is kept, and who may see it.

Applied example, hypothetical. The matrix says the controller may pay recurring bills up to 10,000 dollars; any new payee needs the founder's approval; any investment outside the IPS ranges needs a written note and two family signatures; and no one may approve a payment to themselves or a related party. A fraud through a fake new payee, one of the most common in family offices, now needs two people to fail.

Some family offices that serve more than one family, or that receive fees, may themselves fall within licensing or registration rules. If your office ever manages money for relatives outside your immediate family, or for anyone else, ask a lawyer whether that changes its regulatory status.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, on engagement letters and on the office's regulatory status; accountant, on the approval matrix and payment controls.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming every adviser owes you a duty to put your interests first, so a conflicted recommendation is accepted as neutral advice. The control is a written statement from each adviser of the standard they accept and every way they are paid, in the engagement letter.

The beginner's mistake

Running a family office on trust alone, without an approval matrix. The beginner lets one person pay bills, add payees and report on payments, which is the internal version of the Madoff structure.

Callback

In Week 90, Tessa set out a trustee's duties: loyalty, care, and impartiality among beneficiaries. That is the strongest form of fiduciary duty, and it is the benchmark against which to measure every other adviser. When an adviser declines to accept a duty close to that, it is not necessarily disqualifying, but you now know how much of the checking is yours.

Recap

Advisers owe duties of different strengths, from fiduciary to suitability to little more than honesty. Conflicts must be disclosed and managed. Confirm licences, insist on independent custody, and fix scope, duty, pay and records in the engagement letter. Inside the office, run an approval matrix, a conflicts register and a records rule.

Next: Nadia, on The Numbers: reverse engineering the portfolio a family needs from the spending it wants.
checklist: Each adviser has told me in writing which standard of duty they accept.
Each adviser discloses every form of compensation, including referral payments.
I have confirmed each adviser's licence for the service and jurisdiction.
My assets are with an independent custodian whatever the minimum rule.
Every engagement letter fixes scope, duty, pay, conflicts, reports and termination.
My family office has a written approval matrix with two signatures for new payees.
Nobody approves a payment to themselves or a related party.
head: Field checklist
speak: Not every adviser owes you the same duty. A fiduciary must act loyally in your interest and manage conflicts; trustees and directors owe this. Many advisers are held to a suitability standard instead, meaning the recommendation must fit you, not that it must be the best for you. Which standard applies depends on the licence, the service and the jurisdiction, so ask each adviser in writing. Conflicts of interest, such as commissions and referral payments, must be disclosed, and disclosure only tells you a conflict exists; it does not remove it. Confirm licences before engaging anyone, and keep assets with an independent custodian whatever the minimum rule. The engagement letter fixes scope, duty, pay, conflicts, custody, reports and termination. Inside your own office, run an approval matrix with two signatures for new payees, a conflicts register for family and advisers, and a records rule.
terms: Fiduciary duty — a legal obligation to act loyally in another's interest, avoid or manage conflicts and take care.
Suitability standard — a requirement that a recommendation fit the client's circumstances, without necessarily being the best option for the client.
Approval matrix — a written table of who may approve which decisions, up to what amount, and which need more than one signature.

hostile.q: I'm your investment adviser and I've looked after you well for years. Why do you now want my standard of duty and my fees in writing?
hostile.a: Because my family office now applies the same rule to every adviser, including the ones I trust most. It protects you as well as me: if a recommendation is ever questioned, the record shows exactly what you agreed to do and how you were paid.

title: Reverse Engineering the Portfolio From the Life It Must Fund
summary: Start from the finished outcome, a family's annual spending, and work backward to the portfolio needed, the real return it must earn after fees, tax and inflation, and the project profits that would build it. Every number is a hypothetical, illustrative assumption.
body:
Most people ask how much their money will grow. Reverse the question: start from the life the money must fund, work back to the portfolio required, and you learn which assumption, fees, inflation or return, matters most.

Recall

Q. What are the five functions of a family office?

A. Policy, investment, accounting and reporting, adviser management, and administration. Any arrangement that performs them deliberately is a family office, whatever its size.

Q. When an estate holds assets in two currencies, which currency should cash for estate costs be held in?

A. The currency in which the costs will fall due, so an exchange rate move cannot force a sale of long-term assets to pay them.

Q. If you size a position so that a total loss would cost 5 percent of net worth, what have you decided?

A. The worst case you are willing to accept from that one decision, independent of how confident you feel about it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, an investment policy statement needs a return objective, and that objective should come from what the money must do, not from what a market happened to return last year. Reverse engineering gives you the number. It also tells you, in dollars, what a fee or an inflation assumption is worth, which is the most useful single figure in any conversation with an adviser. Every rate here is an illustrative assumption for arithmetic, not a forecast or a recommendation; a licensed adviser is required before you act.

Step 1: the finished outcome

A hypothetical family wants to spend 200,000 dollars a year, in today's money, for 30 years, from a portfolio, with nothing left at the end. That spending is after personal tax.

Step 2: gross up for tax

Assume, purely for illustration, that withdrawals bear an average tax of 25 percent. The family must withdraw enough that 75 percent of it equals 200,000 dollars. 200,000 divided by 0.75 is about 266,700 dollars a year, before tax.

Step 3: decide the real return

A real return is a return after inflation: what the money gains in purchasing power. Working in real terms lets us keep the spending figure in today's dollars throughout.

Illustrative assumptions: a gross portfolio return of 6.0 percent, inflation of 2.5 percent, and total cost of ownership, all fees together, of 1.0 percent. Real return after costs is roughly 6.0 minus 2.5 minus 1.0, which is 2.5 percent a year. This simple subtraction is an approximation; it is close enough for planning.

Step 4: the portfolio required

We need the sum that, earning 2.5 percent real, can pay 266,700 dollars a year for 30 years and run out at the end. That is the present value of an annuity. The annuity factor, the multiplier that converts a level annual payment into the lump sum needed today, at 2.5 percent for 30 years is about 20.93.

Portfolio required: 266,700 times 20.93, which is about 5,580,000 dollars.

Say that out loud now.

Step 5: test the assumptions backward

Now reverse each assumption, one at a time, and see what it costs.

Fees. Cut total cost from 1.0 to 0.5 percent, so the real return is 3.0 percent. The annuity factor becomes about 19.60. Portfolio required: 266,700 times 19.60, about 5,230,000 dollars. Half a percent of fees is worth about 350,000 dollars of capital the family no longer needs.

Inflation. Keep fees at 1.0 percent, but let inflation run at 3.5 percent instead of 2.5. Real return falls to 1.5 percent, the factor rises to about 24.02, and the portfolio required is about 6,400,000 dollars. One extra point of inflation costs about 820,000 dollars.

Forever instead of 30 years. If the family wants the capital to last indefinitely and pass to the next generation intact in real terms, the portfolio must be the payment divided by the real return. At 2.5 percent: 266,700 divided by 0.025 is about 10,670,000 dollars. Making the money permanent almost doubles the requirement.

The ranking is the lesson. Permanence matters most, then inflation, then fees. Yet fees are the one item fully under the family's control, which is why they deserve attention out of proportion to their size.

A second reverse: the reserve before the portfolio

One more backward step that families often miss. A portfolio funding a life cannot be the same money used for project equity calls, because a capital call that arrives in a falling market forces a sale at the worst time. So reverse from the obligations first. Suppose the family expects to commit up to 800,000 dollars of equity to projects over the next three years, and wants two years of spending, 2 times 266,700, about 533,000 dollars, held in cash or near-cash so a bad market year never forces a sale. Together that is about 1,330,000 dollars that sits outside the long-term portfolio altogether.

Add it to the requirement. The family now needs about 5,580,000 dollars in the long-term portfolio plus 1,330,000 dollars in the reserve tiers, about 6,910,000 dollars in total. That is the liquidity tier idea from Week 85, turned from a principle into a figure. The reserve earns less, and that cost is the price of never being a forced seller.

Step 6: back to the projects

Finally, reverse once more, to the developer's own business. Suppose the family has 1,500,000 dollars invested today and, setting the reserve aside for the moment, the target for 30 years of spending is 5,580,000 dollars. The shortfall is about 4,080,000 dollars, in today's money.

If each completed project leaves the family a hypothetical 1,000,000 dollars of after-tax profit that can be moved out of the business into the portfolio, the family needs about four more such projects, plus growth on the money already invested. That tells you something useful: the plan does not need a single spectacular deal, it needs four ordinary ones completed without a loss. A loss on one project of 1,000,000 dollars adds a fifth.

It also tells you what to protect. The portfolio cannot fund the life until that money leaves the project companies, where it is exposed to project risk and guarantees. The family office's job, and the IPS, should say how and when profits move out.

Step 7: write the result into the policy

The IPS now states: purpose, fund 200,000 dollars a year of after-tax spending in today's money; return objective, at least 2.5 percent real after all costs; cost ceiling, 100 basis points total; and a note that the requirement is sensitive to inflation and should be re-run each year. An adviser proposing a strategy can be measured against those lines.

Professional sign-off required: licensed investment adviser, on return assumptions and allocation; tax adviser, on the effective tax on withdrawals.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a return objective chosen by feel, often by last year's market, so the portfolio is either too small for the life it must fund or invested too aggressively to reach it. The control is to derive the objective from the spending, test it against fees, inflation and permanence, and re-run it every year.

The beginner's mistake

Mixing nominal and real numbers: spending in today's dollars against a return that includes inflation. The result looks comfortable and is wrong by years of spending. Keep both sides real, or both nominal, never one of each.

Callback

In Week 11, Nadia taught the time value of money and net present value: a dollar later is worth less than a dollar now. The annuity factor in this lesson is that same idea applied to a life rather than a building. The portfolio required is simply the present value of the spending you want, discounted at the real return you can expect.

Recap

Start from spending, gross it up for tax, choose a real return after costs, and use an annuity factor to find the portfolio. Test fees, inflation and permanence backward, then reverse once more to the number of projects needed. Write the result into the IPS.

Next: Warrick, on The Room: the quarterly adviser review, and how to replace an adviser who has drifted.
checklist: I state the spending the portfolio must fund, after tax, in today's money.
I gross up withdrawals for an assumed tax rate confirmed with my tax adviser.
I work in real returns after inflation and after all costs.
I find the required portfolio with an annuity factor, not a guess.
I test fees, inflation and permanence one at a time.
I translate the shortfall into a number of ordinary projects.
My IPS return objective and cost ceiling come from this calculation.
head: Field checklist
speak: Reverse engineer the portfolio from the life it must fund. A hypothetical family wants 200,000 dollars a year after tax, in today's money, for 30 years. At an assumed 25 percent tax, it must withdraw about 266,700 a year. Assume 6 percent gross return, 2.5 percent inflation and 1 percent total fees: about 2.5 percent real. The annuity factor at 2.5 percent for 30 years is about 20.93, so the portfolio needed is about 5,580,000 dollars. Now reverse each assumption. Half a point lower fees saves about 350,000 dollars of capital. A point more inflation costs about 820,000. Making the money last forever nearly doubles the need, to about 10,670,000. Against 1,500,000 already invested, the shortfall of about 4,080,000 is roughly four ordinary projects completed without a loss. Write the return objective and a fee ceiling into the investment policy statement.
terms: Real return — the return on money after inflation, measuring the gain in purchasing power.
Annuity factor — the multiplier that converts a level annual payment over a period into the lump sum needed today at a given return.
Return objective — the return a portfolio must earn, stated in an investment policy statement, derived from what the money must fund.

hostile.q: You want a portfolio that earns 2.5 percent after inflation. Why not aim higher and need less capital?
hostile.a: Because aiming higher means taking more risk, and the spending does not stop when markets fall. I would rather build the capital the calculation requires through ordinary projects than depend on a return I may not get. If returns come in higher, the surplus is a margin, not a plan.

title: The Quarterly Review, and Replacing an Adviser Who Has Drifted
summary: A realistic scene: a hypothetical quarterly review with an investment manager whose portfolio has drifted outside the investment policy statement and whose fees have quietly risen. The lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, when to stay silent, and how to end a relationship cleanly.
body:
A quarterly review is not a performance chat. It is a check of one document, the investment policy statement, against one reality, the custodian's statement, and the adviser's job is to explain every gap between them.

Recall

Q. What single structural control would have exposed the Madoff fraud for any one investor?

A. An independent custodian sending statements directly to the investor, reconciled each quarter to the manager's reports.

Q. What is the first thing an executor usually needs to act on foreign assets?

A. Authority recognised in that jurisdiction, through a local grant of probate or recognition of the home grant, together with an accurate register of what and where the assets are.

Q. Why should a developer cap how much of net worth sits in any one project?

A. Because a single project failure, with guarantees behind it, could otherwise damage most of the balance sheet at once.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the hardest part of managing advisers is not hiring them; it is reviewing them honestly once you like them. This scene is hypothetical. You chair a quarterly review of the family's 6,000,000 dollar portfolio. Present: the investment manager, a pleasant and competent person you have worked with for five years, and your accountant, who has prepared a reconciliation from the custodian's statements. The figures are illustrative.

Preparing the room

Before the meeting your accountant sends you one page. Three findings. First, equities are now 72 percent of the portfolio against an IPS range of 50 to 65 percent, because they rose and nobody rebalanced. Second, a new fund was added last quarter, managed by the adviser's own firm, with a higher fee. Third, total cost of ownership has moved from about 110 basis points to about 135.

You decide your one outcome before you walk in: the portfolio returns inside the policy, or the relationship ends. You decide your three open points: the timing of the rebalance, whether the new fund stays at a smaller size, and how fees are reset.

The scene

The manager opens with good news. "It's been a strong quarter. You're up well ahead of the benchmark."

You say: "Thank you. Before performance, I want to go through the policy, line by line, against the custodian's numbers. Then we'll come back to returns."

The manager: "Of course. The equity weight is a bit high, but honestly, it's been working. I'd let it run."

The question behind the question

The manager is not really arguing about equities. He is asking whether the policy is real or decorative: whether you will enforce what you signed. If you let this pass, every future drift will be argued the same way, after the fact, when it is working.

And the new in-house fund carries a question he will not ask aloud: will you notice that he is now paid twice on the same money?

Say that out loud now.

Lines to say

"The policy says 50 to 65. We're at 72. I'd like a plan to bring it inside the range by the end of next month, and your view on how to do that efficiently."

"I see a new fund from your own firm. Please send me, in writing, what your firm earns from it, why you chose it over an outside option, and what the total cost of ownership is with it included."

"Our total cost has gone from about 110 to about 135 basis points. I need it back under the 120 ceiling in our policy. What can you propose?"

"I value the work you've done. This is about the policy, not about you."

Lines never to say

"Well, as long as it's making money." It tells the manager that performance overrides policy, which means risk limits only apply when they are not needed.

"I trust you, so let's not worry about the fees." Trust is why you review, not a reason to stop.

"I'm thinking of moving to someone else" as a bargaining tactic you do not mean. It damages the relationship whether or not you leave.

And never ask the manager to explain the reconciliation your accountant prepared. The reconciliation is independent precisely because the manager did not produce it.

When to stay silent

After you ask what the firm earns from its own fund, stop and wait. The first answer is often a summary; the silence draws out the detail. After he proposes a rebalance plan, let your accountant speak first, because she will check it against the custodian's data before you react to it.

The second hard moment

Midway through, the manager says: "If you rebalance now you'll pay tax on the gains. I'm saving you money by leaving it." That may be partly true, and it deserves a real answer rather than a reflex.

Say: "That's a fair point. Please put it in writing, with an estimate of the tax cost of rebalancing now against the risk of staying at 72. I'll ask my tax adviser to check it. We can also rebalance with new money and income rather than sales." You have accepted the legitimate concern, refused to let it become a permanent exemption from the policy, and moved the decision onto paper where it can be checked by someone without a fee interest.

Never say: "Fine, leave it then." A tax argument that wins once wins every quarter, and the range in the policy becomes decorative.

Holding your state

You may feel awkward correcting someone who has, by the headline numbers, done well for you. That awkwardness is the very pressure that lets drift accumulate. Keep your voice level, keep returning to the document, and speak in terms of the policy rather than the person. If you feel yourself softening, look at the one outcome you wrote down.

If it ends

Suppose the manager declines to rebalance, defends the in-house fund and will not reduce fees. Then you replace him, cleanly. Say: "Thank you for five years. We've decided to move the mandate. Our accountant will coordinate the transfer with the custodian; please don't sell anything in the meantime unless we instruct it." Then confirm in writing the end date, the instruction not to trade, the return of any records you are entitled to, and the final fee calculation.

Because the assets sit with an independent custodian in your own entities' names, the move is an instruction to the custodian, not a negotiation with the manager. That is Rule 94 paying for itself. If the assets had been held by the manager's firm, you would be asking the person you are firing to hand over your money.

Before appointing a replacement, run the selection as you would any procurement: two or three candidates, the same written questions, each one's stated standard of duty and every form of pay, and references from clients of similar size.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is letting performance excuse a breach of policy, so risk limits erode in good years and the family discovers its true risk in a bad one. The control is to review against the IPS and the custodian's records before discussing returns, every quarter, with an independent reconciliation.

The beginner's mistake

Reviewing only performance against a benchmark. The beginner never asks whether the portfolio is still the one the policy describes, or what it now costs, so a strong quarter hides drift and fee creep at once.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught how to handle a hostile question: acknowledge, bridge, answer. Here you are the one asking hard questions, and the same discipline applies in reverse. Acknowledge the good result, bridge to the policy, then ask the specific question and wait for a specific answer.

Recap

Prepare with an independent reconciliation, decide your one outcome and your open points, review policy before performance, ask in writing about in-house products and fee creep, stay silent after the hard questions, and replace a drifted adviser with a written instruction to the custodian.

Next: Kema, on Quiz and Recap: six questions on the family office and a Red Pen on a draft investment policy statement.
checklist: I receive an independent reconciliation from the custodian's records before every review.
I decide my one required outcome and my open points before the meeting.
I review the portfolio against the IPS before discussing performance.
I ask in writing what an adviser earns from any in-house product.
I compare total cost of ownership with the IPS ceiling every quarter.
I never let a strong quarter excuse a breach of policy.
If I replace an adviser, I instruct the custodian in writing and order no trading in between.
head: Field checklist
speak: A quarterly review checks one document, the investment policy statement, against one reality, the custodian's statement. In a hypothetical review, your accountant's reconciliation shows equities at 72 percent against a 50 to 65 percent range, a new fund from the manager's own firm, and total cost up from about 110 to about 135 basis points. Decide your one outcome before the meeting: back inside the policy, or the relationship ends. When the manager leads with strong performance, thank him and turn to the policy line by line. Ask for a rebalance plan, ask in writing what his firm earns from its own fund, and ask how fees return under the ceiling. Never say it is fine as long as it makes money. Stay silent after the hard question. If he will not comply, replace him with a written instruction to the independent custodian. Because you hold the assets, leaving is an instruction, not a negotiation.
terms: Policy drift — the gradual movement of a portfolio outside the ranges in its investment policy statement, often from market moves or unreviewed additions.
Rebalancing — buying and selling to bring a portfolio's allocation back within its policy ranges.
Mandate — the written authority given to an investment manager to manage a defined pool of money under stated rules.

hostile.q: I've beaten the benchmark three years running. You're really going to fire me over an allocation range?
hostile.a: I'm not firing you over returns. I'm asking you to manage inside the policy we both signed and the fee ceiling in it. If you can bring the allocation back inside the range and the cost under the ceiling, I'd like to keep working with you. If you can't, I'll move the mandate.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 94 Review: The Family Office, the Policy and the Advisers
summary: Six questions on the family office with answers, a recap of the week, a Red Pen drill on a draft investment policy statement, and a two-minute boardroom drill explaining how a family's wealth is governed.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: a family office is five functions governed by a written investment policy statement, with policy, management, custody and reporting kept in different hands and every fee counted.

Recall

Q. In the fee example, why did a 75 basis point adviser fee become 160 basis points?

A. Because underlying fund fees, custody and trading, and reporting were layered on the same money. The total cost of ownership was more than double the quoted fee.

Q. What is incapacity planning?

A. Arranging, through powers of attorney and similar documents, who acts for you while you are alive but unable to decide, so your affairs and businesses do not freeze.

Q. What does concentration mean when most of your net worth is in one building?

A. That one event affecting that building, its market or its tenants can damage most of your wealth at once.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, if you can answer these six questions aloud without notes, you can chair your own wealth review and hold every adviser to a standard you set. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What makes an arrangement a family office?

Answer: Performing five functions deliberately for the family's wealth as a whole: policy, investment, accounting and reporting, adviser management and administration. Size, staff and premises are optional.

Question 2. What seven questions does an investment policy statement answer?

Answer: What the money is for; the return needed after fees, tax and inflation; the loss that can be tolerated; what must stay liquid and when; the constraints; the allocation ranges; and who reviews it, how often and against what benchmark.

Question 3. What was the root cause of the Madoff fraud, and what rule follows?

Answer: One firm managed, held and reported on its clients' money, so the only evidence the money existed came from the manager. Rule 94: never let the person who manages your money also hold it or report on it; use an independent custodian whose statements reach you directly and are reconciled quarterly.

Question 4. What is total cost of ownership, and why does it differ from a quoted fee?

Answer: Every cost of holding and managing the assets as one annual figure. It differs because fees are layered: adviser, underlying funds, custody, trading and reporting all charge the same money.

Question 5. What is the difference between a fiduciary duty and a suitability standard?

Answer: A fiduciary must act loyally in your interest and manage conflicts. A suitability standard, in general terms, only requires that a recommendation fit your circumstances. Which applies depends on the adviser's licence, the service and the jurisdiction.

Question 6. How do you reverse engineer the portfolio a family needs?

Answer: Start from after-tax spending in today's money, gross it up for tax, choose a real return after all costs, and multiply the annual withdrawal by the annuity factor for the period. Add reserve tiers for spending and project calls, then test fees, inflation and permanence.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Warrick and Nadia defined the family office as five functions and introduced the investment policy statement. Ford and Roman took the Madoff case, exposed in December 2008, giving Rule 94. Nadia priced fees in basis points, showed how layers compound, and when consolidation pays. Omar set out duties, conflicts, licensing, custody and the office's own approval matrix. Nadia reverse engineered a portfolio from a family's spending. Warrick ran a quarterly review and the replacement of a drifted manager.

The Red Pen

Here is a hypothetical excerpt from a draft investment policy statement. Find the defects before reading on.

Investment Policy Statement, Family Holdings. Purpose: to grow the family's wealth. Return objective: to beat the market. Risk: moderate. Liquidity: as needed. Allocation: at the manager's discretion. Custody: assets will be held by the Manager for convenience. Reporting: the Manager will provide an annual summary of performance. Fees: the Manager's standard fee applies. Review: as required.

The defects. First, the purpose is a slogan; it says nothing about what the money must fund, so no return objective can be derived from it. Second, "beat the market" names no market, no benchmark and no period, and has nothing to do with the family's needs; the objective should be a real return after costs taken from the spending calculation. Third, "moderate" risk is undefined; the policy needs a loss the family can tolerate in money and in time. Fourth, "liquidity as needed" ignores the reserve tiers for spending and project equity calls. Fifth, allocation at the manager's discretion removes the ranges that make drift visible. Sixth, and most serious, custody with the manager is precisely the structure behind Rule 94. Seventh, an annual summary from the manager is neither independent nor frequent; reporting should be quarterly and reconciled to an independent custodian. Eighth, "standard fee" hides layering; the policy should cap total cost of ownership in basis points. Ninth, "review as required" means never; set a schedule and name who reviews.

The corrected version would state the spending it funds, a real return objective, a loss tolerance, a liquidity schedule, allocation ranges, an independent custodian, quarterly reconciled reporting, a total cost ceiling, and a dated review by named people.

Kema's note on reading any policy: ask of every line, "could a stranger tell, from the custodian's statement alone, whether this line was obeyed?" If not, the line is an opinion, not a rule. Purpose, risk, liquidity and review in this draft all fail that test. A good IPS can be audited by someone who has never met the manager, which is exactly the property that would have protected Madoff's investors.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a relative who asks, "Who actually looks after the family's money, and how do we know it's safe?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Nobody looks after it alone. A written investment policy statement says what the money is for, what return it needs after fees and inflation, how much loss we can tolerate, what stays in cash, and the ranges for each kind of asset. The manager invests within those rules. An independent custodian holds the assets in our own names and sends statements directly to our accountant, who reconciles them to the manager's reports every quarter. Every adviser tells us in writing what duty they accept and every way they are paid, and we cap the total cost. Each quarter we check the portfolio against the policy before we talk about performance. If an adviser drifts, we instruct the custodian to move the mandate. That way the money's safety does not depend on trusting any one person."

Score yourself. Did you name the policy first? Did you separate management from custody and reporting? Did you mention cost? Did you finish inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is concentrating trust in one adviser, so the same person decides, holds and reports. The control is structural: separation of duties, independent custody and a quarterly reconciliation.

The beginner's mistake

Writing an investment policy statement in adjectives. A policy that cannot be measured cannot be enforced, and a policy that cannot be enforced is decoration.

Callback

In Week 82, Vera taught document control and contemporaneous records: the record made at the time is the record that wins. A family office runs on the same principle. The custodian's statement, the reconciliation and the dated policy are the contemporaneous records; the manager's summary is a later account of them.

Recap

Run five functions, govern them with a measurable policy, keep duties separate, count every fee, know each adviser's duty and pay, derive the return objective from the spending, and review policy before performance. Rule 94 keeps custody independent.

Next: Elias, on First Principles: the personal tax lifecycle, from salary and dividends to retirement income.

What seven questions does an investment policy statement answer?
What was the root cause of the Madoff fraud, and what rule follows?
What is total cost of ownership, and why does it differ from a quoted fee?
What is the difference between a fiduciary duty and a suitability standard?
How do you reverse engineer the portfolio a family needs?
head: The six questions
speak: This week's core: a family office is five functions, not a building: policy, investment, accounting and reporting, adviser management and administration. The investment policy statement states what the money is for, the real return it needs after costs, the loss it can tolerate, its liquidity, constraints, allocation ranges and review. The Madoff fraud, exposed in December 2008, survived because one firm managed, held and reported on its clients' money. Rule 94: never let the person who manages your money also hold it or report on it; use an independent custodian and reconcile quarterly. Fees are layered, so count total cost of ownership in basis points and compound it before calling anything cheap. Advisers owe duties of different strengths, from fiduciary to suitability, so get the standard and every source of pay in writing. Derive the portfolio from the spending it must fund, and review policy before performance.
terms: Consolidated report — one statement combining every entity and account a family holds, showing total assets, debts, costs and performance.
Benchmark — a stated index or measure against which a portfolio's performance is judged, chosen in advance in the policy.
Reconciliation — checking one record against an independent one, such as a manager's report against a custodian's statement, and explaining every difference.

hostile.q: We're a small family. Isn't an investment policy statement and an independent custodian overkill for a few million dollars?
hostile.a: The custodian costs a few basis points and removes the single most damaging risk, the manager controlling the evidence. The policy is two pages and stops us deciding in a panic. At a few million dollars, one avoidable mistake costs more than both for decades.
